questions.text: Which description captures the core difference between LoRA and full fine-tuning?

options.A: LoRA freezes the base weights and trains low-rank adapter matrices.
options.B: LoRA changes only the prompt while leaving all parameters untrained.
options.C: LoRA trains every base weight but discards optimizer states after each step.
options.D: LoRA replaces the base model with a database of training examples.

questions.explanation: LoRA learns a low-rank update through smaller trainable matrices while keeping the original weights frozen.

questions.text: A square 1024-by-1024 projection receives a rank-8 LoRA adapter. Ignoring biases, how many trainable adapter parameters does this add?

options.A: 8,192, because only one 1024-by-8 matrix is trained.
options.B: 1,048,576, because the entire projection must be updated.
options.C: 16,384, from two matrices with 1024 times 8 parameters each.
options.D: 1,064,960, because both base and adapter weights are trained.

questions.explanation: The two adapter matrices have 1024×8 and 8×1024 entries, totaling 16,384 trainable parameters; the base remains frozen.

questions.text: LoRALayer computes (x @ A @ B) * (alpha / rank). A is random and B is all zeros at initialization. What does LinearWithLoRA return before training?

options.A: A random perturbation of the base output because A is random.
options.B: The base linear output, because the adapter contribution is zero.
options.C: An all-zero output, because B also zeros the frozen base path.
options.D: The base output multiplied by alpha / rank on both paths.

questions.explanation: The adapter product is zero because B is zero, so adding it preserves the frozen linear layer’s original output.
